explanation.body: To maintain contact, the object's maximum downward acceleration cannot exceed $g=9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Since $a_{\max}=\omega^2 x_0$, the limiting amplitude is $x_0=g/(2\pi f)^2=9.81/[2\pi(1.5)]^2=0.11\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.B: Divides by angular frequency only once.
perOption.C: Divides by the ordinary frequency without converting or squaring it.
perOption.D: An amplitude of 9.0 m would require a peak downward acceleration far greater than gravity.

difficultyReason: The contact condition must be identified before applying the SHM acceleration formula.
misconception: Ignoring the limit on downward acceleration

explanation.body: For a point source, $I\propto 1/r^2$, and wave intensity satisfies $I\propto A^2$, where $A$ is the amplitude. Hence $A\propto 1/r$, so doubling the distance reduces the amplitude from $8X$ to $4X$.

perOption.A: Assumes the amplitude stays constant as the wave spreads.
perOption.C: Applies the inverse-square law directly to amplitude.
perOption.D: Reduces amplitude by a factor of eight, which would require an inverse-cube dependence.

difficultyReason: It combines two standard proportionalities to obtain the amplitude ratio.
misconception: Applying the inverse-square law directly to amplitude

explanation.body: The grating spacing is $d=1/(3.0\times10^5)\ \mathrm{m}$. From $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$, the upper bound on the order is $d\sin90^\circ/(600\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m})=5.6$, so the largest integer order is 5. Counting five orders on each side and the central image gives $2(5)+1=11$.

perOption.A: Counts only the nonzero orders on one side.
perOption.B: Counts only four orders on each side and omits the central image.
perOption.C: Stops at the fourth order on each side before adding the central image.

difficultyReason: The calculation requires finding the last allowed integer order and counting the maxima on both sides.
misconception: Confusing maximum diffraction order with the total number of maxima

explanation.body: For one strand, $R=\rho l/A=(1.72\times10^{-8})(1.0)/[\pi(0.30\times10^{-3}/2)^2]=0.2433\ \Omega$. For seven identical strands in parallel, $1/R_{\parallel}=7/R$, so $R_{\parallel}=0.03476\ \Omega$. The potential difference is $V=IR_{\parallel}=13(0.03476)=0.4519\ \mathrm{V}\approx0.45\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the cable resistance by a factor of about 100, as when the diameter is taken ten times too large.
perOption.B: Uses the strand diameter as the radius, making its area four times too large.
perOption.D: Applies the total cable current to the resistance of a single strand.

difficultyReason: It requires finding the area of one strand, combining parallel resistances, and applying Ohm’s law.
misconception: Using diameter as radius or ignoring parallel strands

explanation.body: With the switch open, $I=0$, so $V=\mathcal E-Ir$ gives $\mathcal E=1.5\ \mathrm{V}$. With the switch closed, $I=0.75/4.0\ \mathrm{A}$, so $0.75=1.5-(0.75/4.0)r$. This gives $r=4.0\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: With this resistance and the closed-switch current, the internal voltage drop would be only 0.19 V.
perOption.B: Using the full e.m.f. across the 4.0 Ω load doubles the calculated current and halves the inferred internal resistance.
perOption.D: Uses the 8.0 Ω setting from the open-switch case to calculate current after closing the switch.

difficultyReason: It requires reading the open-circuit voltage and then finding the current through the closed circuit.
misconception: Using the disconnected load to calculate current

explanation.body: The electric field points in the direction of the force on a positive test charge and is tangent to the field line at $X$. An electron is negatively charged, so its force points along that tangent in the opposite direction to the field.

perOption.A: Points up and left along a line that is not tangent to the field line at X.
perOption.C: Points down and right along a line that is not tangent to the field line at X.
perOption.D: Follows the electric field, which gives the force direction for a positive charge.

issues: The worked solution labels the answer “And: B”. The answer table also prints B.
difficultyReason: It requires identifying the local tangent and reversing its direction for a negative charge.
misconception: Using the field direction as the force direction for an electron
transcription:
The diagram shows an electric field pattern caused by two positive and two negative point charges of equal magnitude placed at the four corners of a square.

In which direction does the force act on an electron at point $X$?

[The top-left and bottom-right corners are positive, and the top-right and bottom-left corners are negative. Curved field lines with arrows run from positive to negative charges. Point $X$ lies inside the square on a line linking the left-hand charges. Four arrows start at $X$.]

A Up and to the left
B Almost vertically up, slightly to the right
C Down and to the right
D Almost vertically down, slightly to the left

explanation.body: As the particle enters moving to the right, its path curves upwards, so the centripetal magnetic force is upwards. Fleming’s left-hand rule gives a conventional current in the same direction as the particle’s velocity, so the charge is positive. An undeflected particle needs a downward electric force, which requires a downward electric field for a positive ion.

perOption.A: An upward field on a positive ion reinforces the upward magnetic force.
perOption.C: An electron entering to the right would curve downwards in this magnetic field.
perOption.D: An electron entering to the right would curve downwards, contrary to the path shown.

difficultyReason: The entry curvature gives the force direction, which must then be used to infer the charge and balance the forces.
misconception: Reversing the magnetic force on a positive charge
transcription:
A particle is in a region of uniform magnetic field. The field is directed into the plane of the page. The path of this particle is shown in the figure below.

[Crosses show a uniform magnetic field into the page within a square region. The particle enters from the left moving to the right and follows a curve that bends upwards, as indicated by an arrow on the path.]

What is this particle and what is the direction of the electric field for it to pass through with no deflection?

A A positive ion, upwards
B A positive ion, downwards
C An electron, upwards
D An electron, downwards

explanation.body: The coil moves within a uniform field with its area and orientation fixed, so its magnetic flux linkage does not change. By Faraday’s law, the induced e.m.f. is zero.

perOption.B: Treats the coil’s translational speed as a rate of change of flux linkage.
perOption.C: Introducing a cosine factor does not create a flux-linkage change during translation.
perOption.D: The sine factor describes the fixed projection of the coil area, so the flux linkage still has zero rate of change.

difficultyReason: It tests whether translating a coil through a uniform field changes its flux linkage.
misconception: Assuming any motion across field lines induces a net e.m.f.
transcription:
A plane coil of wire containing $N$ turns each of area $A$ is placed so that the plane of the coil makes an angle $\theta$ with the direction of the uniform magnetic field of flux density $B$. The coil is now moved through a distance $x$ in time $t$ to the position shown dotted.

[Plan view of the uniform field. Equally spaced horizontal field arrows point right. The solid oblique line represents the plane of the coil and makes an angle $\theta$ with the field. The dotted line is parallel to the solid line and displaced downwards by $x$.]

What is the e.m.f. induced in the coil?

A Zero
B $NAB\frac{x}{t}$
C $NABx\frac{\cos\theta}{t}$
D $NABx\frac{\sin\theta}{t}$

explanation.body: The peak current is $I_0=\sqrt{P_0/R}=\sqrt{150/6.0}=5.0\ \mathrm{A}$. Because $P=I^2R$, the current period is twice the power period, so $T=0.020\ \mathrm{s}$. Substituting gives $I=I_0\sin(2\pi t/T)=5.0\sin(100\pi t)$.

perOption.B: Uses the power period as the current period.
perOption.C: Uses the peak value of current squared as the peak current.
perOption.D: Uses 25 A as the amplitude and an angular frequency that does not match the zero crossings.

difficultyReason: It requires extracting the peak power and recognising that current takes two power cycles to repeat.
misconception: Equating the periods of power and current
transcription:
The graph shows the variation with time $t$ of the power $P$ dissipated in a resistor of resistance $6.0\ \Omega$ when it is connected to an alternating supply.

[The graph plots $P/\mathrm{W}$ against $t/\mathrm{s}$. Three identical peaks reach $150\ \mathrm{W}$, and the power is zero at $0$, $0.010$, $0.020$ and $0.030\ \mathrm{s}$.]

Which equation represents the sinusoidal alternating current through the resistor?

A $I=5.0\sin(100\pi t)$
B $I=5.0\sin(200\pi t)$
C $I=25\sin(100\pi t)$
D $I=25\sin(300\pi t)$

explanation.body: Electrons with $12.5\ \mathrm{eV}$ can excite hydrogen from the ground state up to $n=3$. Using $\lambda=hc/\Delta E$, the $3\to2$ transition gives about $6.65\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$, in the visible range. The $3\to1$ and $2\to1$ transitions give $1.03\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$ and $1.22\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$ respectively, both outside the visible range.

perOption.A: Misses the visible line from the transition between levels 3 and 2.
perOption.C: Counts an additional line even though both transitions to the ground state are ultraviolet.
perOption.D: Counts all three transitions without checking their wavelengths.

issues: For the 3→2 line the key gives 665 nm, while its displayed rounded numerator divided by 1.87 eV gives about 663 nm. Both values are visible.
difficultyReason: It requires finding the highest accessible level and checking each possible transition against the visible range.
misconception: Counting all emission lines as visible

explanation.body: At the cutoff, the maximum photon energy satisfies $hc/\lambda_{\min}=eV_a$, where $V_a$ is the accelerating voltage. Increasing $V_a$ therefore decreases the minimum wavelength.

perOption.B: Reverses the inverse relationship between the cutoff wavelength and the accelerating voltage.
perOption.C: Assumes raising the voltage necessarily adds characteristic peaks, which depend on the available transitions in the target.
perOption.D: Treats the characteristic wavelengths as voltage-dependent even though they are set by energy level differences in tungsten.

issues: The extracted text duplicates option A and shifts the distractors. The explanation uses the options printed in the question image.
difficultyReason: The accelerating voltage is related to the maximum photon energy and hence the wavelength cutoff.
misconception: Confusing the X-ray cutoff with the characteristic peaks

explanation.body: From $\Delta mc^2=E_\gamma$, the mass difference is $\Delta m=(2.13\times10^{-13})/(3.00\times10^8)^2=2.366667\times10^{-30}\ \mathrm{kg}$. Using $1\ \mathrm{u}=1.66\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$ gives $\Delta m=0.0014257\ \mathrm{u}$. The excited-state mass is $59.9308\ \mathrm{u}+\Delta m=59.9322\ \mathrm{u}$.

perOption.A: Makes the excited state lighter than the ground state and uses too large a mass difference.
perOption.B: Subtracts the photon’s mass equivalent from the ground-state mass.
perOption.D: Adds a mass increment about twice that implied by the emitted photon energy.

difficultyReason: It requires converting the photon energy to a mass difference in atomic mass units and choosing the correct sign.
misconception: Subtracting the emitted photon’s mass equivalent from the ground-state mass
transcription:
Nuclei of atoms can exist in excited states. When an excited nucleus returns to its state of lowest energy (the ground state), a $\gamma$-ray photon may be emitted.

The mass of a nucleus in its ground state is $59.9308\ \mathrm{u}$. The energy of the photon emitted when this nucleus returns from an excited state to the ground state is $2.13\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$.

What is the mass of the nucleus in the excited state?

A $59.9208\ \mathrm{u}$
B $59.9294\ \mathrm{u}$
C $59.9322\ \mathrm{u}$
D $59.9337\ \mathrm{u}$

explanation.body: Tin-124 is stable, so after one $60$-day half-life the antimony-to-tin ratio is $1:1$. After two half-lives, $\tfrac14$ of the original antimony remains and $\tfrac34$ has become tin, so the ratio is $1:3$. After three half-lives the fractions are $\tfrac18$ and $\tfrac78$, giving $1:7$. The tin-to-antimony ratio therefore reaches $6$ between 120 and 180 days.

perOption.A: Between 60 and 120 days the ratio rises only from 1 to 3.

difficultyReason: It requires tracking the stable daughter nuclei as well as the undecayed parent nuclei.
misconception: Taking the initial number of parent nuclei as the denominator
transcription:
Antimony-124 undergoes radioactive decay, with a half-life of 60 days, to become tin-124. Tin-124 is stable.

Initially, a sample of antimony-124 contains no tin-124.

After what period of time will the ratio $\frac{\text{number of tin-124 nuclei}}{\text{number of antimony-124 nuclei}}$ equal 6?

A Between 60 days and 120 days
B 120 days
C Between 120 days and 180 days
D 180 days

explanation.body: The factor $1/(e^{hf/(kT)}-1)$ is dimensionless, so $[D^3]=[R][c^2]/[h]$. The units of $R$, $c^2$ and $h$ are $\mathrm{J\,s^{-1}\,m^{-2}/Hz}$, $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$ and $\mathrm{J\,s}$ respectively. These give $\mathrm{s^{-3}}$ for $D^3$, hence $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ for $D$.

perOption.A: Gives units of force, although mass and length cancel in the unit calculation.
perOption.C: Gives units of energy, which cancel between R and Planck’s constant.
perOption.D: Gives the units of the cube of D without taking the cube root.

difficultyReason: It requires interpreting a compound unit and isolating the units of a cubed quantity.
misconception: Reporting the units of the cube instead of the quantity
transcription:
Planck’s Law of black body radiation is given by

$R=\frac{2h(D)^3}{c^2}\times\frac{1}{e^{hf/(kT)}-1}$

where $R$ is power per unit area per unit frequency, $h$ is Planck’s constant, $c$ is the speed of light in a vacuum, $f$ is frequency of electromagnetic radiation, $k$ is Boltzmann’s constant, $T$ is the thermodynamic temperature, and $D$ is an unknown physical quantity.

Which of the following shows the correct units for $D$?

A $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$
B $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$
C $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$
D $\mathrm{s^{-3}}$

explanation.body: The momentum is $p=(52.000)(10.0)/(0.63-0.00)=825.397\ \mathrm{g\,cm\,s^{-1}}$. Add the absolute timing uncertainties to get $0.02\ \mathrm{s}$, then add the fractional uncertainties: $\Delta p/p=0.001/52+0.1/10+0.02/0.63=0.041765$. The absolute uncertainty is $34.5\ \mathrm{g\,cm\,s^{-1}}$, which rounds to $30\ \mathrm{g\,cm\,s^{-1}}$ at one significant figure, so report $p=(830\pm30)\ \mathrm{g\,cm\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Using only one timing uncertainty can give an uncertainty of 20 after rounding.
perOption.C: Underestimates the propagated uncertainty and keeps two significant figures in it.
perOption.D: Rounds the uncertainty to two significant figures instead of one.

difficultyReason: It combines absolute uncertainties in a time difference, fractional uncertainties in a quotient, and consistent rounding.
misconception: Using only one timing uncertainty or rounding to inconsistent places
transcription:
The momentum $p$ of a rubber ball of mass $m$, as it rolls across a table surface at constant speed is given by the equation $p=\frac{mL}{t_2-t_1}$, where

$t_1$ is the time at which the front end of the ball passes point P,
$t_2$ is the time at which the front end of the ball passes point Q.

[The front of the ball is at the dashed line through P. A second dashed line through Q lies to its right, and the horizontal distance from P to Q is labelled $L$.]

Data from an experiment to determine $p$ is recorded as follows:

$m=(52.000\pm0.001)\ \mathrm{g}$
$L=(10.0\pm0.1)\ \mathrm{cm}$
$t_1=(0.00\pm0.01)\ \mathrm{s}$
$t_2=(0.63\pm0.01)\ \mathrm{s}$

The momentum of the rubber ball should be recorded as

A $(830\pm20)\ \mathrm{g\,cm\,s^{-1}}$
B $(830\pm30)\ \mathrm{g\,cm\,s^{-1}}$
C $(825\pm28)\ \mathrm{g\,cm\,s^{-1}}$
D $(825\pm35)\ \mathrm{g\,cm\,s^{-1}}$
